topic: Closing Files and Handling Cleanup Errors

questions.question: Why should a file be closed, and where should `defer f.Close()` be placed?
questions.title: Closing files with defer
questions.direct_answer: Closing a file releases its operating-system handle and finalizes the file's lifecycle. In a short function, place a deferred close immediately after a successful open so every later return runs cleanup. Never defer a method on a nil file after an open error, and do not discard close errors when successful output must be guaranteed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Check the open error before arranging cleanup.
Place `defer f.Close()` immediately after a successful open in a bounded function.
Deferred calls run when the surrounding function returns.
Closing releases the handle; it does not replace read, write, or flush checks.
Output code may need to merge or return the close error.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An open `*os.File` owns an operating-system resource. Closing it releases that handle; repeatedly forgetting close can eventually exhaust the process limit. Cleanup must be arranged only after the open error is nil, because a failed open does not provide a usable file.

In a short function that owns one file, the usual shape is open, check, then defer close immediately. The defer belongs near acquisition and still runs if parsing or validation returns early. It runs at function return, not at the end of the nearest if block.

For example, a helper that reads the first line can open the path, defer close, scan one record, and return from several error branches without duplicating cleanup. For a read-only helper, a primary read error normally carries the important failure, although a close error can still be handled according to the API contract.

Output needs greater care because a deferred `f.Close()` by itself throws its returned error away. When the caller needs proof that all output completed, I check write and buffer-flush errors and capture the close error, often through an explicit close or a deferred function that joins it with the named return error.

sections.title: Ownership starts only after Open succeeds
sections.content:
The resource lifecycle is acquire, use, and release. Error handling divides acquisition from ownership: before a successful return there is nothing valid to close; afterward the current function must either close the file or transfer ownership through a documented API.

Defer makes release follow every return path, but it does not interpret the result of the deferred call. Whether a close error matters depends on whether the file was input, output, or part of a larger transaction.

sections.title: Defer guarantees timing, not error policy
sections.content:
A deferred call is scheduled when execution reaches the defer statement. Its receiver and arguments are evaluated then, while the call itself runs just before the surrounding function returns. That is why the statement belongs after the nil-error check and close to the matching open.

A bare `defer f.Close()` is concise for many read paths, but it ignores the returned error. A writing function can use a named error and a deferred closure to combine close failure with an earlier error. The caller then receives one honest result rather than a false success.

sections.title: Safe ownership sequence
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Call os.Open] --> B{err is nil?}
  B -- No --> C[Return open error]
  B -- Yes --> D[Own file handle]
  D --> E[Arrange Close]
  E --> F[Use file]
  F --> G[Function returns]
  G --> H[Deferred Close runs]
```

questions.question: Why can `defer` inside a long loop exhaust file descriptors?
questions.title: Defer scope inside loops
questions.direct_answer: A deferred call waits until its surrounding function returns, not until the current loop iteration ends. If one long-running function opens thousands of files and defers every close, all those handles remain live together. Put one iteration in a helper function with its own defer, or explicitly close before continuing when immediate release is clear and safe.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `defer` is function-scoped, not block- or iteration-scoped.
A long loop can keep every opened handle live until the outer return.
Move one iteration into a helper to give each defer a short lifetime.
Explicit close is valid when every branch handles it correctly.
The same pattern applies to response bodies, rows, and other resources.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Defer is tied to the function invocation that executes it. A defer written inside a for loop does not run at the closing brace of that iteration. If the outer function keeps processing, every successfully opened file stays open until that function finally returns.

This becomes a resource-growth bug when the input can contain many paths or the loop is a long-lived worker. Memory may look normal while the process accumulates file descriptors and eventually receives a too-many-open-files error. The problem is lifetime, not the cost of the defer statement itself.

For example, an import job can call a `processFile` helper for each path. The helper opens one file, defers its close, processes the record, and returns. Its defer runs before the next outer iteration starts, so the maximum number of open input files remains roughly one.

Explicit close at the bottom of the loop can also work, but every continue, break, and error return must preserve it. I prefer the helper boundary when processing is nontrivial because the function scope states ownership clearly and keeps cleanup correct as branches are added.

sections.title: Resource lifetime follows function lifetime
sections.content:
Lexical indentation can make an iteration look like a lifetime boundary, but defer does not use that boundary. It records work on the current function's defer stack and executes it only as that call returns.

A small helper is more than style: it creates the release point the algorithm needs. The outer loop manages the collection, while the helper owns exactly one resource and guarantees that it is released before returning.

sections.title: Bound concurrency and lifetime separately
sections.content:
Moving work into a helper bounds sequential lifetime. If iterations run concurrently, each worker may still own a file, so the concurrency limit also bounds descriptors. A worker pool or semaphore can keep that number within the service's resource budget.

The pattern generalizes to `http.Response.Body`, database rows, temporary files, and locks. Ask which function owns the resource and when that function returns. The answer reveals whether defer releases promptly enough.

sections.title: Two loop shapes and their live handles
sections.content:
| Shape | When Close runs | Peak handles for N sequential items |
|---|---|---:|
| Defer in the outer loop | Outer function return | Up to N |
| Helper with one defer | End of each helper call | About 1 |
| Bounded worker pool | End of each worker task | Up to worker count |

questions.question: Why must write, flush, and close errors all be checked?
questions.title: Completing a file write safely
questions.direct_answer: A successful Write only confirms what that call accepted. Buffered bytes can still fail during `Flush`, operating-system state can fail during `Sync` when durability is required, and `Close` can report finalization errors. A writing function should return the first meaningful failure and also preserve a close error instead of using a bare deferred close that silently discards it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Check each write result and do not assume the full payload was accepted.
Flush a `bufio.Writer` before closing its underlying file.
Use `Sync` only when the durability contract requires it.
Check `Close` for output files rather than discarding its error.
Return or join cleanup failure without hiding the earlier operation error.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Output completion has layers. A Write can fail immediately or accept fewer bytes. A `bufio.Writer` may accept data into memory even though the later transfer to the file fails, so `Flush` is a required operation and its error must be returned.

Closing releases the file and can report a final error. A bare `defer file.Close()` runs reliably but throws that result away. A function that reports success while close failed has broken its output contract, especially for files that will be published, uploaded, or used as durable state.

For example, a report writer can use a named return error. It defers a closure that joins the eventual close error, writes through a buffered writer, checks Flush, and calls `file.Sync()` only if the requirement includes pushing current file data to stable storage as defined by the platform.

`Sync` is not automatically required for every cache or temporary file, and even it is not a complete transactional replacement protocol. I define whether the caller needs buffered delivery, file durability, or atomic publication, then check the operations that establish that exact guarantee.

sections.title: Success moves outward through several buffers
sections.content:
Application bytes may first enter a bufio buffer, then the operating-system file state, and later durable storage. Write, Flush, Sync, and Close address different boundaries. Skipping an operation can be correct only when the API's required boundary stops before it.

Error precedence matters too. If writing already failed and close also fails, the caller needs the primary cause without losing evidence of cleanup failure. Modern Go code can combine them with `errors.Join`.

sections.title: State the durability promise before choosing operations
sections.content:
Flush moves pending bytes from a `bufio.Writer` to its wrapped writer; it does not close that writer. Closing an `*os.File` does not know about a separate bufio wrapper and therefore cannot flush that wrapper for you. The correct order is write, flush, optional sync, then close.

Atomic replacement is another concern. A robust design may write a sibling temporary file, validate and sync it, close it, then rename it, with directory durability and platform behaviour considered separately. `os.WriteFile` or one successful Close alone does not make a multi-step update transactional.

sections.title: Output completion boundaries
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Application bytes] -->|Write| B[bufio memory]
  B -->|Flush| C[os.File / kernel]
  C -->|Sync when required| D[durability boundary]
  C -->|Close| E[handle released]
  B -. Close file does not flush wrapper .-> E
```
